front: What are the lecture’s three legal bases for patient mobility?
back: Treaty freedom-of-services case law, Regulation 883/2004 and Directive 2011/24/EU. They must not be reduced to one set of conditions. Source: Frischhut — Economic rights (2026/27); PDF pp. 3–17, 19–34.

front: What is passive provision of services?
back: The recipient crosses the border to receive the service; patient mobility is the relevant course example. Source: Frischhut — Economic rights (2026/27); PDF pp. 3–17, 19–34.

front: What does proportionality add to a legitimate objective?
back: A measure must be appropriate and not go beyond what is necessary; simply naming public health does not complete the analysis. Source: Frischhut — Economic rights (2026/27); PDF pp. 3–17, 19–34.

front: What is harmonisation in this lecture?
back: Creating similar legal standards, distinguished from removing national barriers through fundamental freedoms. Source: Frischhut — Economic rights (2026/27); PDF pp. 3–17, 19–34.

front: Expand AAAQ.
back: Availability, accessibility, acceptability and quality. Source: Frischhut — Human rights (2026/27); PDF pp. 5, 10–26, 36–46.

front: What are the four dimensions of accessibility in the lecture?
back: Non-discrimination, physical accessibility, economic accessibility and information accessibility. Source: Frischhut — Human rights (2026/27); PDF pp. 5, 10–26, 36–46.

front: Name the three levels of state obligation discussed.
back: Respect, protect and fulfil. Fulfil also encompasses facilitating, providing and promoting. Source: Frischhut — Human rights (2026/27); PDF pp. 5, 10–26, 36–46.

front: Why distinguish “can” from “should” in the vaccination discussion?
back: Whether an interference can be justified legally differs from whether a policy is ethically preferable in its context. Source: Frischhut — Human rights (2026/27); PDF pp. 5, 10–26, 36–46.

front: What is direct discrimination?
back: An expressly applied protected ground is used for different treatment, subject to the relevant legal framework. Source: Frischhut — Non-discrimination: short summary; PDF pp. 1–4.

front: What is indirect discrimination?
back: A neutral-looking criterion can produce a disadvantage linked to a protected ground; evidence and context matter. Source: Frischhut — Non-discrimination: short summary; PDF pp. 1–4.

front: What two comparison patterns can raise discrimination issues?
back: Different rules for comparable situations; the same rule for relevantly different situations. Source: Frischhut — Non-discrimination: short summary; PDF pp. 1–4.

front: Does naming public health complete the justification?
back: No. The short summary also requires evidence and necessity; the relevant framework and proportionality matter. Source: Frischhut — Non-discrimination: short summary; PDF pp. 1–4.

front: What does the lecture mean by morality?
back: Shared norms of right and wrong conduct in a social setting; ethical reflection can examine these norms. Source: Frischhut — Values and ethics (2026/27); PDF pp. 8–9, 17–21, 24–30, 36–37.

front: Name examples of operating principles in the health-values discussion.
back: Quality, safety, evidence and ethics, patient involvement, redress, privacy and confidentiality. Source: Frischhut — Values and ethics (2026/27); PDF pp. 8–9, 17–21, 24–30, 36–37.

front: Why is solidarity relevant to financing?
back: The 2006 discussion connects solidarity to arrangements that support accessibility for all. Source: Frischhut — Values and ethics (2026/27); PDF pp. 8–9, 17–21, 24–30, 36–37.

front: What is the Eurobarometer reading trap?
back: Personal values and values associated with the EU are different questions, and the slides show historical waves. Source: Frischhut — Values and ethics (2026/27); PDF pp. 8–9, 17–21, 24–30, 36–37.

front: How does the course classify the four countries?
back: Bismarck: Netherlands and Austria. Beveridge: Italy and Norway. These are teaching families, not identical systems. Source: Frischhut — Organizational issues (2026/27); PDF pp. 9–15, 18–22.

front: What four functions help organise a system reading?
back: Raising funds, pooling risks and money, purchasing or allocating care, and delivering services. This is the Hub’s study scaffold. Sources: De Belvis et al. — Italy: Health System Summary (2024), PDF pp. 3–7, 15; Bachner et al. — Austria: Health System Summary (2024), PDF pp. 3–7, 15; OECD/European Observatory — Austria: Country Health Profile (2025), PDF pp. 14–15.

front: Why can a tax-based system include private providers?
back: Financing and provider ownership are different questions, as the assigned country readings illustrate. Sources: De Belvis et al. — Italy: Health System Summary (2024), PDF pp. 3–7, 15; Bachner et al. — Austria: Health System Summary (2024), PDF pp. 3–7, 15; OECD/European Observatory — Austria: Country Health Profile (2025), PDF pp. 14–15.

front: What should accompany every statistic?
back: Its source, reference year, definition, unit and denominator; state when comparisons are not like-for-like. Sources: De Belvis et al. — Italy: Health System Summary (2024), PDF pp. 3–7, 15; Bachner et al. — Austria: Health System Summary (2024), PDF pp. 3–7, 15; OECD/European Observatory — Austria: Country Health Profile (2025), PDF pp. 14–15.

front: What is community rating in the historical readings?
back: A given basic insurance product does not charge different premiums according to the individual’s health risk; the precise historical rules are source-dated. Source: van de Ven, van Kleef & van Vliet — Risk selection threatens quality of care (2015); Health Affairs 34:1713–1720; supplied PDF pp. 2–8.

front: What is the risk-selection concern?
back: Predictable undercompensation can make some groups less financially attractive, encouraging actions that undermine intended cross-subsidies. Source: van de Ven, van Kleef & van Vliet — Risk selection threatens quality of care (2015); Health Affairs 34:1713–1720; supplied PDF pp. 2–8.

front: Define a subgroup predictive ratio in the 2015 article.
back: Average predicted expenditure divided by average actual expenditure. Below one indicates undercompensation, but the choice of subgroup matters. Source: van de Ven, van Kleef & van Vliet — Risk selection threatens quality of care (2015); Health Affairs 34:1713–1720; supplied PDF pp. 2–8.

front: Why is the 2008 paper not a current insurance guide?
back: It is a historical reform account with period-specific amounts, arrangements and forecasts. Source: van de Ven, van Kleef & van Vliet — Risk selection threatens quality of care (2015); Health Affairs 34:1713–1720; supplied PDF pp. 2–8.

front: What does SSN stand for?
back: Servizio Sanitario Nazionale, the Italian National Health Service. Source: De Belvis et al. — Italy: Health System Summary (2024); Supplied PDF pp. 3–7, 10–20.

front: What does LEA identify in the report?
back: The national benefits package: Livelli essenziali di assistenza. Source: De Belvis et al. — Italy: Health System Summary (2024); Supplied PDF pp. 3–7, 10–20.

front: What is a key Italian governance tension in the reading?
back: A national entitlement is implemented through regionally organised systems with uneven resources and access. Source: De Belvis et al. — Italy: Health System Summary (2024); Supplied PDF pp. 3–7, 10–20.

front: Why distinguish domestic mobility from EU cross-border mobility?
back: Moving between Italian regions and moving between countries involve different institutional and legal questions. Source: De Belvis et al. — Italy: Health System Summary (2024); Supplied PDF pp. 3–7, 10–20.

front: Why does Norway still need priority setting in the chapter?
back: Even a comprehensive and relatively well-funded system faces finite capacity and competing demands. Source: Hagen & Feiring — Health Policy Reforms for Three Decades: Then Returning to Square One? (2025); Oxford Handbook of Norwegian Politics, ch. 31; supplied PDF pp. 2–10.

front: What is activity-based financing?
back: Funding related to treatment activity, discussed alongside global budgets and its intended and unintended incentives. Source: Hagen & Feiring — Health Policy Reforms for Three Decades: Then Returning to Square One? (2025); Oxford Handbook of Norwegian Politics, ch. 31; supplied PDF pp. 2–10.

front: What is the accountability tension?
back: Delegation can support expertise and consistency but may narrow public contestation of difficult allocation choices. Source: Hagen & Feiring — Health Policy Reforms for Three Decades: Then Returning to Square One? (2025); Oxford Handbook of Norwegian Politics, ch. 31; supplied PDF pp. 2–10.

front: Is the chapter a full system manual?
back: No. It explicitly focuses on reforms, efficient and fair resource use, and priority-setting debates. Source: Hagen & Feiring — Health Policy Reforms for Three Decades: Then Returning to Square One? (2025); Oxford Handbook of Norwegian Politics, ch. 31; supplied PDF pp. 2–10.

front: Who shares responsibility in the Austrian readings?
back: Federal government, Länder and social-insurance/provider institutions, with different roles across sectors. Source: OECD/European Observatory — Austria: Country Health Profile (2025); Supplied PDF pp. 2–3, 9–10, 14–22.

front: What does “wait or pay” illustrate?
back: Very broad formal coverage can coexist with unequal waiting and out-of-pocket experiences. Source: OECD/European Observatory — Austria: Country Health Profile (2025); Supplied PDF pp. 2–3, 9–10, 14–22.

front: Why not treat 2024 and 2025 report percentages as an automatic trend?
back: Underlying data years, definitions and denominators can differ. Source: OECD/European Observatory — Austria: Country Health Profile (2025); Supplied PDF pp. 2–3, 9–10, 14–22.

front: What is the digital-health study lesson?
back: Inputs such as spending and infrastructure need to be distinguished from actual use and benefits. Source: OECD/European Observatory — Austria: Country Health Profile (2025); Supplied PDF pp. 2–3, 9–10, 14–22.

front: Distinguish de lege lata and de lege ferenda.
back: The existing framework versus a proposed future framework; identify which is being discussed. Source: Frischhut — European Health Union workshop (2026/27); PDF pp. 3–10, 12–13, 17–26.

front: What does One Health connect in the workshop?
back: Human, animal and environmental health perspectives. Source: Frischhut — European Health Union workshop (2026/27); PDF pp. 3–10, 12–13, 17–26.

front: What are the two assigned workshop preparation documents?
back: The European Health Union manifesto and the 2006 Council conclusions on common health-system values and principles. Source: Frischhut — European Health Union workshop (2026/27); PDF pp. 3–10, 12–13, 17–26.

front: What makes a useful original workshop proposal?
back: A defined need and group, a relevant value, a practical measure, an accountable actor, a trade-off and a way to examine implementation. Source: Frischhut — European Health Union workshop (2026/27); PDF pp. 3–10, 12–13, 17–26.

front: Why distinguish legislative competence from an individual right?
back: The power to adopt a measure and the right a person can invoke are different legal questions; the lecture analyses both. Source: Frischhut — Economic rights (2026/27); PDF pp. 11, 21–25 and 29.

front: What does the Directive outline add beyond reimbursement?
back: Responsibilities of treatment and affiliation states, contact points, and cooperation including prescriptions, reference networks and related health-policy fields. Source: Frischhut — Economic rights (2026/27); PDF pp. 11, 21–25 and 29.

front: Why does a finding of no jurisdiction not settle proportionality?
back: It concerns whether the court may address the questions presented, not whether the interference is substantively justified. Source: Frischhut — Human rights (2026/27); PDF pp. 23–24, 33–36 and 41–46.

front: What safeguards should accompany a Vavřička summary?
back: Retain the source’s discussion of medical exceptions, sanctions, remedies, safety monitoring and absence of forced administration to the applicants. Source: Frischhut — Human rights (2026/27); PDF pp. 23–24, 33–36 and 41–46.

front: What should precede a direct/indirect discrimination label?
back: Identify the relevant comparator, criterion, protected ground and legal framework; explain the evidence for any indirect effect. Source: Frischhut — Non-discrimination: short summary; PDF pp. 1–4.

front: What are the two proportionality questions emphasised in the summary’s approach?
back: Can the measure achieve the legitimate aim, and is there a less restrictive way of doing so? Apply them within the relevant legal framework. Source: Frischhut — Non-discrimination: short summary; PDF pp. 1–4.

front: Why is trust not a substitute for implementing a principle?
back: The diagram frames trust as an overarching goal; the argument must still explain the concrete practices meant to support it. Source: Frischhut — Values and ethics (2026/27); PDF pp. 8–9, 17–21 and 26–30.

front: What are the four biomedical ethics principles named in the diagram?
back: Respect for autonomy, nonmaleficence, beneficence and justice. The slide lists them without providing a universal numerical balancing rule. Source: Frischhut — Values and ethics (2026/27); PDF pp. 8–9, 17–21 and 26–30.

front: Can private delivery coexist with public financing?
back: Yes. The Italy report describes public and accredited private providers within the SSN; financing and ownership are different dimensions. Source: De Belvis et al. — Italy: Health System Summary (2024); PDF pp. 3–8.

front: Why compare entitlement separately from practical access?
back: A service can be included while waiting, geography, cost or local capacity still prevents timely use. Source: De Belvis et al. — Italy: Health System Summary (2024); PDF pp. 3–8.

front: What is the article’s predictive-ratio definition?
back: Average predicted healthcare expenditure divided by average actual expenditure for the selected group; group construction matters to interpretation. Source: van de Ven, van Kleef & van Vliet — Risk selection threatens quality of care (2015); PDF pp. 4–5.

front: Why does reducing a compensation gap not necessarily eliminate selection?
back: A residual predictable gap can remain even after a large percentage reduction; improvement and elimination are different claims. Source: van de Ven, van Kleef & van Vliet — Risk selection threatens quality of care (2015); PDF pp. 4–5.

front: What does LEA identify in the Italy report?
back: The nationally guaranteed package of services; it does not itself show identical local capacity or waiting times. Source: De Belvis et al. — Italy: Health System Summary (2024); PDF pp. 3–8.

front: Why should the financing source not replace an account of provider payment?
back: The report combines taxation with different methods of paying local authorities, GPs, specialists and hospitals. Source: De Belvis et al. — Italy: Health System Summary (2024); PDF pp. 3–8.

front: Which three priority criteria does the supplied chapter describe?
back: Expected benefit, severity and cost-effectiveness, with differences in how they are used at clinical and group levels. Source: Hagen & Feiring — Health Policy Reforms for Three Decades: Then Returning to Square One? (2025); PDF pp. 7–9.

front: Why is a shorter hospital stay not a complete coordination outcome?
back: The chapter also reports concerns about municipal burden, premature discharge and rehabilitation after leaving hospital. Source: Hagen & Feiring — Health Policy Reforms for Three Decades: Then Returning to Square One? (2025); PDF pp. 7–9.

front: What does the wait-or-pay dilemma describe?
back: The profile’s contrast between waiting for covered contracted care and paying for potentially faster non-contracted care, with reimbursement limits. Source: OECD/European Observatory — Austria: Country Health Profile (2025); PDF pp. 14–20.

front: Why do digital investment, provider adoption and patient use need separate indicators?
back: They describe different stages of implementation; high spending alone does not establish widespread usable access. Source: OECD/European Observatory — Austria: Country Health Profile (2025); PDF pp. 14–20.

front: What are the four connected components of the workshop’s proposed update?
back: An EHU framing, a purpose-driven preamble, a cumulative set of core values, and principles that operationalise those values. Source: Frischhut — European Health Union workshop (2026/27); PDF pp. 3–10 and 24–26.

front: What does de lege ferenda signal in the workshop?
back: Future-oriented proposals for development, distinct from describing the existing framework under de lege lata. Source: Frischhut — European Health Union workshop (2026/27); PDF pp. 3–10 and 24–26.

front: What is capitation’s payment unit?
back: A listed person, not each visit. Source: Rosella Levaggi — Italy health system guest lecture (2026); PDF pp. 9–11.

front: Why can equal capitation produce unequal margins?
back: Resource needs and costs differ across patients. Source: Rosella Levaggi — Italy health system guest lecture (2026); PDF pp. 10–11.

front: What unit does the simplified DRG account use?
back: A classified case with payment relative to a reference. Source: Rosella Levaggi — Italy health system guest lecture (2026); PDF pp. 12–13.

front: Name a DRG trade-off in the lecture.
back: Possible efficiency versus strategy, innovation and quality concerns. Source: Rosella Levaggi — Italy health system guest lecture (2026); PDF pp. 14–15.

front: What connects national standards and regional finance?
back: LEA commitments and equalisation alongside regional revenues and organisation. Source: Rosella Levaggi — Italy health system guest lecture (2026); PDF pp. 17–19.

front: Which ASL account combines purchasing and production?
back: The programmer account. Indirect reimbursement outside contracts is not automatic. Source: Rosella Levaggi — Italy health system guest lecture (2026); PDF p. 26.

front: What border is central to the Italian mobility discussion?
back: The border between Italian regions, not necessarily an international border. Source: Rosella Levaggi — Italy health system guest lecture (2026); PDF pp. 30–32.

front: Why keep the fiscal-residuum table dated?
back: It cites 2009 and cannot establish current regional balances. Source: Rosella Levaggi — Italy health system guest lecture (2026); PDF p. 37.

front: What are the three historical pillars?
back: Contribution-based financing, corporatist self-administration and occupational grouping. Source: Lukas Kerschbaumer — Austria health system guest lecture (2026); PDF pp. 7–8.

front: What does path dependency explain?
back: How established national institutions condition responses to European pressures and opportunities. Source: Lukas Kerschbaumer — Austria health system guest lecture (2026); PDF pp. 9–10.

front: Why is fund count not a complete merger evaluation?
back: It is a structural measure, not proof of savings or full harmonisation. Source: Lukas Kerschbaumer — Austria health system guest lecture (2026); PDF p. 11.

front: Why is cross-setting coordination difficult?
back: Responsibility and financing are split across actors and budgets. Source: Lukas Kerschbaumer — Austria health system guest lecture (2026); PDF pp. 12 and 19.

front: 80% of what in the private-care example?
back: Of the contracted reference rate, not automatically of the private invoice. Source: Lukas Kerschbaumer — Austria health system guest lecture (2026); PDF p. 13.

front: What does the service-coverage chart measure?
back: Government and compulsory financing shares by service category, not personal entitlements. Source: Lukas Kerschbaumer — Austria health system guest lecture (2026); PDF p. 23.

front: What status does the digital-first sequence have?
back: A lecture-described reform strategy and targets, not established complete implementation. Source: Lukas Kerschbaumer — Austria health system guest lecture (2026); PDF pp. 24–26.

front: How should contradictory slide statistics be treated?
back: Flag differences in number, year or denominator; do not silently correct or memorise a disputed figure. Source: Lukas Kerschbaumer — Austria health system guest lecture (2026); PDF pp. 19 and 21–22.

front: Which level handles primary and long-term care?
back: Municipal government in the lecture’s institutional account. Source: Terje P. Hagen — Norway health system guest lecture (2026); PDF pp. 4–7.

front: What is the somatic specialist-grant mix?
back: 70% need-adjusted capitation and 30% activity financing, with research grants separate. Source: Terje P. Hagen — Norway health system guest lecture (2026); PDF pp. 18–20.

front: How does 70/30 react to 20% more activity in an invented 100-unit model?
back: 70+30×1.2=106, assuming only the activity part scales. Source: Terje P. Hagen — Norway health system guest lecture (2026); PDF pp. 18 and 43.

front: What are the GP income’s two views?
back: 50/50 capitation/service method;50/20/30 municipal/state/patient payer view. Source: Terje P. Hagen — Norway health system guest lecture (2026); PDF pp. 25–26.

front: Is the municipal stairway compulsory for every patient?
back: No. It illustrates support settings, not an individual clinical rule. Source: Terje P. Hagen — Norway health system guest lecture (2026); PDF pp. 27–30.

front: What does the ceiling graph demonstrate?
back: A cap on eligible payments in a simplified framework, without establishing a current actual ceiling amount. Source: Terje P. Hagen — Norway health system guest lecture (2026); PDF pp. 37–38.

front: What complements length of stay in reform evaluation?
back: Readmissions, mortality, capacity, continuity and differences between patient groups. Source: Terje P. Hagen — Norway health system guest lecture (2026); PDF pp. 52–56.

front: Why use PDF rather than printed slide numbers?
back: Printed numbers diverge from PDF positions near the end; consistent locators avoid ambiguity. Source: Terje P. Hagen — Norway health system guest lecture (2026); PDF pp. 64–73.
